1. **Explain** how connecting observations makes their grouping and order easier to see.

2. **Distinguish** which observations belong to the same series from the order in which they should be connected.

3. **Use** temporal encodings to arrange observations chronologically, and **compare** line and area charts for ordered data.

4. **Explain** how stacking changes the interpretation of a chart and when a shared baseline is more useful.

Some data has a natural order to it,
e.g. temporal variables such as which year or time of the day
a data point was recorded.

In the chart below,
we can see how the CO2 emissions have changed over time
for the worlds continents.
As you can see,
the chart applies the strategies we have learned so far
and uses color to group observations from different continents.
But the overlap from the different groups
make it difficult to follow the development over time
for any particular continent and the chart is a bit confusing
even after studying it for a while.
How do you think you could change this chart
to make it easier to see how the CO2 emissions for each continent change over time?

```{python setup}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

alt.data_transformers.enable('vegafusion')
```

```{python bad-points}
#| echo: false
years = range(1900, 2030, 8)
co2_per_capita = pd.read_csv('data/co-emissions-per-capita.csv').query('Year.isin(@years)')
points = alt.Chart(co2_per_capita, width=450).mark_point().encode(
    x='Year:T',
    y=alt.Y('CO2_emissions_per_capita').title('Tonnes of CO2 per capita'),
    color=alt.Color('Entity').title(None)
)

points
```

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Do you think connected the points belonging to the same continent
would make it easier or harder to spot trends?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

We can use the natural order of the observations
to connect the points that belongs to the same continent with a line.
Drawing a line drawn from the earliest to the most recent year
helps us with two things:
It makes it easier to see the development over time for any single continent
and it makes it easier to see which points belong to which continent.
As such,
a line is a graphical tool that assist both with ordering and with grouping.

```{python line-overlay}
points.mark_line() + points.mark_point(filled=True)
```

:::::

::::

:::

In [Groups](5_groups.qmd), we learned how to distinguish groups of observations.
Now we will look at observations that also have a meaningful order,
and use connections to make that order visible.
Grouping tells us which observations belong together;
ordering tells us which observation comes next within each group.

Connecting observations can help us see a trend,
but the lines in this chapter simply join the supplied values.
In [Trends](11_trends.qmd), we will return to the different task
of estimating a broader pattern with a fitted line or smoother.

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

## Data with a meaningful order

Time provides a natural ordering: each observation has a place in a sequence.
We will use lines and areas to help readers follow that sequence.
The same idea applies beyond time, for example to measurements taken
at increasing doses of a treatment.

### Global development data

We will visualize population and fertility values for successive years from 1800 to 2018.
The data comes from the [Gapminder country-level dataset](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joelostblom/teaching-datasets/main/world-data-gapminder.csv),
but the values for this chapter have already been calculated for us:

- [World population data](data/gapminder_world_trends.csv) has one row per year,
  with the total population of the countries in the source dataset.
- [Regional population and fertility data](data/gapminder_region_trends.csv) has one row per region and year,
  with its total population and the average number of children per woman across its countries.
  Each country contributes equally to that average; it is not weighted by population.

These prepared values let us focus on how to connect observations.
In [Summaries](7_summaries.qmd), we will learn how to calculate values
such as totals from country-level observations.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair

```{python}
#| label: load-order-python
#| tags: []
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd


world = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_world_trends.csv', dtype={'year': str})
regions = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_region_trends.csv', dtype={'year': str})
world
```

We read `year` as text so that Altair can interpret values such as `"1800"`
as calendar years when we use a temporal encoding below.

#### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: load-order-r
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_gray(base_size = 18))

world <- read_csv('data/gapminder_world_trends.csv')
regions <- read_csv('data/gapminder_region_trends.csv')
world
```

:::

When reading in a new dataset,
it is always a good idea to have a look at a few rows
like we did above
to get an idea of how the data looks.

Another helpful practice is to use the `.info()` method
to get an overview of the column types
and see if there are any `NaNs` (missing values).

If there are many missing values in a column,
we would want to look into why that is.
Later in the course, we will learn about how to visualize
missing values to understand if there are patterns
in which values are missing,
which could affect our data analysis.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair

```{python}
#| label: order-info-python
world.info()
regions.info()
```

#### ggplot

In the tidyverse,
we can use `glimpse` to view info of our dataframe.

```{r}
#| label: order-glimpse-r
glimpse(world)
glimpse(regions)
```

:::

Now that we have seen what the data table looks like,
and which data type the values in each column are,
let's think about what we would want to visualize and why.

Since the data reaches all the way back to the 1800s,
it would be really interesting to plot
how the world population has been growing up until today.
We can use a line plot to show this change over time.

## Connecting observations in order

Now we are ready to create our plot!
Since we want to see how the **world** population has changed,
we use `world`, which already contains one population value for each year.
Let's first show each year's value as a point:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: population-points-alt
alt.Chart(world).mark_point().encode(
    x='year:Q',
    y='population'
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: population-points-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_point()
```

:::

The positions already show how population changes from year to year.
Connecting consecutive years makes it easier to follow the sequence
as one continuous series:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: population-line-alt
#| tags: []
alt.Chart(world).mark_line(point=True).encode(
    x='year:Q',
    y='population'
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: population-line-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point()
```

:::

The points have not moved and no new population values have been calculated.
We have added connections between neighboring observations in time.
The line segments guide the eye; they do not establish what the population
was at every unobserved moment between those observations.

The order of connection matters.
Here, Altair's line mark and ggplot's `geom_line()` follow increasing x values
within each series, rather than an arbitrary ordering of rows in the file.
We should connect observations only when those connections have a meaningful interpretation.

Interestingly,
it seems like the world population have been growing in two distinct phases:
slowly before 1950,
and more rapidly afterwards.
This is an example of how making order visible also helps us notice a trend.

### Showing calendar years

In the Altair example, we used `year:Q` to treat the year as a quantitative value.
However, something seems to be going on with the x-axis
as the years are showing up in integer format as `1,990, 2,000, etc`.
While adding the comma as a thousand separator like this generally improves readability,
it is not what we want for years,
which we expect to show up as `1990, 2000, etc`.
We can indicate that we want Altair to use a temporal data type here
by adding the `:T` suffix to the column name.
We will learn more about different data types later,
for now this is all we need.

```{python}
#| label: population-temporal-axis
#| tags: []
alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y='population'
)
```

When the observations are close together, we can omit the point marks
and still follow their order through the line, as in the chart above.

## Areas and multiple ordered groups

We could also have created this same visualization using an area chart:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: population-area-alt
alt.Chart(world).mark_area().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y='population'
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: population-area-gg
ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_area()
```

:::

Both lines and areas preserve the sequence of values over time.
Filling the area down to a zero baseline emphasizes the magnitude of those values,
while a line emphasizes the path through them.
When displaying multiple ordered groups,
lines and areas have different advantages.
Let's see how it looks for the area chart first.

We now use `regions`, which contains a separate population value
for each region in each year.
Region determines which observations belong to the same group,
and year determines their order within that group.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: population-stacked-alt
alt.Chart(regions).mark_area().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y='population',
    color='region'
)
```

### ggplot

`geom_area()` stacks the regional areas by default.
The population values are already in the dataset,
so we can map them directly to the y-axis.

```{r}
#| label: population-stacked-gg
ggplot(regions, aes(x = year, y = population, fill = region)) +
    geom_area()
```

:::

The y-axis range of this chart
is the same as the one on the previous plot,
so it is easy to see how the total world population has changed over time.
From the stacked colored regions,
we also get a rough idea of how each region has grown,
but it is hard to compare exactly,
especially for regions that are not stacked next to each other.
For example,
we can't really tell if Europe or Africa, has the largest population in the most recent year.

Altair stacks by areas by default,
which is usually what we want when creating an area chart with groups.
But if someone saw our chart without knowing this,
they might think that the areas are layered behind each other,
so that we only see the top of the blue region 
peak out behind the orange region.
Using a line chart
is the preferred choice when we want to view the exact values of each group
and don't care as much about the total of the groups added together.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: region-lines-alt
alt.Chart(regions).mark_line().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y='population',
    color='region'
)
```

### ggplot

To change the stacking behavior we can set the position to `dodge`
and add some transparency with the `alpha` parameter.

```{r}
#| label: population-dodged-gg
ggplot(regions, aes(x = year, y = population, fill = region)) +
    geom_area(position = 'dodge', alpha = 0.4)
```

A line plot would be more effective than the layered/dodged area chart above.

```{r}
#| label: region-lines-gg
ggplot(regions, aes(x = year, y = population, color = region)) +
    geom_line()
```

:::

In the chart above,
connections help us follow each region across years without jumping
to another region's observations.
Color identifies the groups, while the connected lines make their sequences visible.

With those separate sequences,
it is immediately clear that Africa has had a bigger population than Europe
and since shortly after the year 2000.
The drawback is that
it's quite cognitively demanding
to try to reconstruct the total world population
by adding all the lines up together,
especially over time!

When the sum of the different groups in the chart is not meaningful,
a line chart is also the better choice.
For example,
let's answer a slightly different question with a visualization:
"What is the average number of children per woman in a country for each continent?"
The `children_per_woman` column in `regions` already contains those averages.
Let's first look at this with an area plot like above:

::: {.column-margin}

**Factual tidbit**

Population experts predict that the world population
will stop increasing and stabilize around 11 billion people.
This is mainly due to improved living conditions in low income countries,
which reduces child mortality
and allows families to have fewer children.
You will learn more about this in lab 1.

:::

```{python}
#| label: fertility-stacked
alt.Chart(regions).mark_area().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y='children_per_woman',
    color='region'
)
```

Here,
summing/stacking the average areas does not give a meaningful number
(there wasn't 30 children per woman in the 1800s...).
We can try to unstack the areas to remedy this issue,
and show them behind each other on the same baseline instead of on top of each other.

#### `alt.X` and `alt.Y`

In order to create an area chart
where the colored regions are layered behind each other 
rather than stacked on top,
we need to leverage the helper functions `alt.Y` and `alt.X`.
These helpers have the role of customizing things like order, groups, and scale for the axis.
When using just `y='column'`,
we're still calling `alt.Y()` under the hood,
we just save ourselves some typing.

Let's first use `alt.Y` on its own
without any additional argument
to recreate the same area plot as above
just to demonstrate how it works.

```{python}
#| label: fertility-axis-helper
alt.Chart(regions).mark_area().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y=alt.Y('children_per_woman'),
    color='region'
)
```

Now we can pass options inside `alt.Y`,
e.g. to turn off stacking
we can use the `.stack(False)` method of `alt.Y`
(we also set the opacity of the areas
to allow us to see area behind each other).

```{python}
#| label: fertility-overlapping
alt.Chart(regions).mark_area(opacity=0.4).encode(
    x='year:T',
    y=alt.Y('children_per_woman').stack(False),
    color='region'
)
```

As you can see,
this is still not a very effective plot
for our data.
It is difficult to discern where
the areas overlap and we mostly see a brown smear
of them all on top of each other;
a line chart would not have this issue.
We will see when layered areas can be effective later in the course,
but generally it is when there are fewer groups,
or non-overlapping areas such as density plots.

In the chart above,
it also looks like the sequences of values over time
for different continents
are pretty similar.
If we create the line chart
of the same data,
we can see that Europe follows a much different development
than to the other regions.

```{python}
#| label: fertility-lines
alt.Chart(regions).mark_line().encode(
    x='year:T',
    y='children_per_woman',
    color='region'
)
```

Note that you could use `stack=True` to create a stacked line chart,
but you should **never** do this
as it it very confusing and unexpected.
If you want to stack groups, use an area chart.

## From connections to summaries

So far, we have used position, grouping, and order to make supplied values easier to read.
But sometimes there are too many observations to show individually,
or the question calls for a total, count, or typical value.
In [Summaries](7_summaries.qmd), we will explore how to reduce a collection
of observations to useful quantities—and ask what information that reduction leaves out.
